extracted.intended_audience: students (advanced undergraduate / beginning graduate) studying Rudin's Principles of Mathematical Analysis; readers solving/challenging supplementary exercises in real analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Produce written solutions and proofs for supplementary exercises accompanying Rudin chapters on series, power series, rearrangements, summation by parts, and continuity; follow the hints and proof-style conventions indicated in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: p-series limit-formula (root-test analog)
rubrics_metrics.description: If p is any positive real number, and we let a_n = n^{-p}, show that - lim_{n→∞} (log a_n)/(log n) = p. If (a_n) be any sequence of positive terms, and let p = - lim sup (log a_n)/(log n). Show that if p > 1, then Σ a_n converges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as an analogue of the root test based on the 'long-term' change in magnitude; the argument uses basic properties of the logarithm. The exercise both asks to compute the limit for the model p-series and to define the p-value for general sequences via the lim sup of log ratios, then apply it to deduce convergence when p>1. (Also see the question 'What happens when we apply this test to a series which the root test shows to converge?')

rubrics_metrics.name: ratio-test analog (successive-term relation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let p = liminf_{n} n(1 - (a_{n+1}/a_n)). Show that if lim_{n→∞} n(1 - (a_{n+1}/a_n)) = p and p > 1, then Σ a_n converges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the analog of the ratio test, based on the relation between successive terms. The text notes this test is generally easier to use than the log-based criterion but cannot handle series whose terms don’t decrease regularly. The proof is said to be hard without differentiation (hence the comment about proof difficulty).

rubrics_metrics.name: slightly modified ratio test (c-step ratio)
rubrics_metrics.description: A series Σ a_n converges if for some positive integer c one has lim sup_{n→∞} |a_{n+c}/a_n| < 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a relaxation of the usual ratio test allowing a step of c instead of 1. The exercises ask to show this condition is satisfied (for c=2) by certain example series. Use lim sup computations as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: radius of convergence via coefficient ratios
rubrics_metrics.description: Let Σ c_n z^n be a power series with all c_n nonzero. If the sequence (|c_n/c_{n+1}|) approaches either a real number or +∞, then that limit equals the radius of convergence of the power series. When the sequence does not approach a limit, obtain inequalities relating lim sup and lim inf of |c_n/c_{n+1}| to the radius of convergence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parts (a)-(c) are said to follow easily from results in Rudin (no heavy new arguments required). Part (d) asks to verify the inequalities on an explicit example where coefficients switch behavior on blocks. Use Rudin's characterization of radius of convergence and the ratio-type relations rather than reinventing general proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: prefer characterization of radius over lim sup formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggestion: Don’t use the 'lim sup' formula for the radius of convergence, but its characterization in terms of where power series converge and where they diverge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explicitly advises using the conceptual characterization (region of convergence / divergence) to deduce properties of radii, rather than applying the lim sup formula mechanically; this is both a pedagogical and practical guideline for constructing elegant solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: power series boundary-behavior examples
rubrics_metrics.description: For a power series with radius R, for |z|=R the series may (i) diverge, (ii) converge non-absolutely, or (iii) converge absolutely. Provide three examples to exhibit these three phenomena (possibly at different boundary points).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The exercise asks explicitly to give three examples and notes that some power series can exhibit two of the phenomena at different boundary points while the remaining phenomenon may require a different series. This is a constructive-examples requirement for full credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: summation by parts / Schwarz inequality hint
rubrics_metrics.description: If Σ a_n converges, so does Σ a_n / n (exercise statement). Suggestion: Write a_n = b_n / n^2 and use the Schwarz inequality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page gives a concrete transformation hint (decompose terms and apply Cauchy-Schwarz). Follow the suggested substitution and inequality technique, and include any short lines that capture a hypothesis used in the exercise.

rubrics_metrics.name: ε-proof preference
rubrics_metrics.description: You should give a careful 'ε'-proof, unless you prove it using some previous result in Rudin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author instructs that solutions should typically be given with explicit ε-δ (or ε-N) arguments, except when a direct citation of an earlier Rudin theorem suffices. This is a stylistic and rigor requirement for presenting solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: grouping-to-absolute-convergence technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a convergent series Σ a_n, define block sums A_k = a_{n_k} + ... + a_{n_{k+1}-1}. Show Σ A_k converges and equals Σ a_n, and show one can choose the block endpoints so that Σ A_k converges absolutely (by comparison with a given convergent series Σ c_k of positive terms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This exercise prescribes the grouping method as a technique for achieving absolute convergence when possible; the hint suggests constructive choice of block boundaries and a comparison-test argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: power series converge absolutely inside radius
rubrics_metrics.description: Let Σ a_n z^n be a power series with radius of convergence R>0. For all complex z with |z|<R the series converges absolutely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part (a) is straightforward and should be shown directly. Part (b) asks to demonstrate different behaviors on the circle |z|=R by examples. Use standard tests (root/ratio/comparison) when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy product rule for absolutely convergent series
rubrics_metrics.description: If Σ a_n = A and Σ b_n = B and these series converge absolutely, then the Cauchy product Σ p_n equals A·B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference Rudin's result (exercise R13) for the statement and use the absolute convergence hypothesis to justify rearrangements and termwise multiplication; apply this in related exercises about radii of convergence of product series.

rubrics_metrics.name: rearrangements: absolute convergence implies invariance
rubrics_metrics.description: If a series Σ a_n has the property that all of its rearrangements converge, it is absolutely convergent. Conversely, if some rearrangement converges, then the original series converges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The exercises ask to prove these implications and to construct explicit rearrangements (e.g., patterns 1,1,-2,1,1,-2,...) showing possible behaviors. Use examples and theorems (Rudin’s Theorem 3.54) to illustrate both positive and negative results about rearrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: mixing-number criterion for safe rearrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: For a permutation (k_n) of the positive integers define the mixing number mix((k_n),N) as the number of same-color blocks when coloring indices ≤N versus >N; prove that the following are equivalent: (i) mix((k_n),N) is bounded as a function of N; (ii) For every convergent series Σ a_n of real numbers, the rearranged series Σ a_{k_n} also converges (and sums agree).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives the combinatorial definition and asks to prove equivalence; note the bound mix ≤ 2N+1 and use it to reason about how permutations interleave early and late terms. Provide proof of equivalence and examples where mix is unbounded to show failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: root-test non-invariance under rearrangement (but convergence persists)
rubrics_metrics.description: Find a series which converges by the root test, and a rearrangement of this series for which the root test gives no information. However, show the rearranged series must still converge and explain why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an exercise in understanding limitations of tests: produce an example where root-test criteria fail to detect convergence after permutation, and provide an argument (independent of root test) showing convergence is preserved.

rubrics_metrics.name: criteria for composing limits (necessary and sufficient)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose f:E→Y with lim_{x→p} f(x)=q and g:F→Z with lim_{y→q} g(y)=r. Then lim_{x→p} g(f(x)) = r if and only if either q∈F and g is continuous at q, or there exists ε>0 such that f does not take the value q at points arbitrarily close to p (equivalently q∈f(N_ε(p)∩E) ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This exercise highlights exactly when one can 'compose' limit-statements. Present the equivalence and prove both directions; use the provided counterexample in the text to motivate the necessity of the additional condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: continuity characterized by sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: A map f:X→Y between metric spaces is continuous if and only if for every sequence (p_n) which converges in X, one has lim_{n→∞} f(p_n) = f(lim_{n→∞} p_n). Equivalently, for every convergent sequence (p_n) in X, the sequence (f(p_n)) converges in Y (and equals f of the limit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The exercise asks to prove the equivalence of the ε-δ definition and sequential characterization of continuity; use the sequential-to-epsilon and epsilon-to-sequential implications carefully (hint provided for (iii)⇒(ii)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy-criterion analog for limits of functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Formulate and prove a necessary and sufficient ε-δ condition for lim_{x→p} f(x) to exist when f:E→Y and Y is a complete metric space, analogous to the statement 'a sequence converges iff it is Cauchy'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The requested formulation should be in ε-δ form (not in terms of sequences). Show the condition is necessary in general and both necessary and sufficient when Y is complete; explain why sufficiency fails if Y is not complete.

rubrics_metrics.name: difficulty tags as expectation indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: Many exercises are annotated with difficulty codes like (d: 1,2,3,4,5) indicating expected difficulty/effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these tags as guidance on how long and how much technique is expected in a solution; use them to decide whether to provide a sketch or a full detailed ε-proof (the text sometimes suggests 'short line' or 'sketch' for easier parts).
